name: macro-method
intent: Keep a method readable as a summary of what happens by restricting its body to calls of well-named methods, each of which performs exactly one step of the computation.
problem: A method that mixes the sequence of operations with the details of each operation cannot be read in one pass: to work out what the method does the reader has to hold conditions, expressions and side effects in mind at once, and every change to a detail begins with re-reading the whole body.
context: Applies to ordinary method bodies in any language with callable procedures, and pays off in code read more often than written: orchestration and use-case methods, algorithm phases, base-class skeletons that subclasses refine, and domain operations whose steps domain experts should recognise. It matters wherever the cost of a reader misreading a method's intent exceeds the cost of a few extra calls.
benefits: The body reads at a single level of abstraction: the call sequence is the specification, and the details live exactly one level down.
Every step acquires a name, so the coordinator communicates intent and each step documents its own contract - names replace comments.
Changes localise: editing a step touches one small method, and a step needed twice can simply be called twice.
Named steps are natural test and override seams: a test can exercise one step, and a subclass can replace a step without copying the sequence.
Tooling gets structure for free - stack traces, debuggers and profilers show one frame and one timer per step.
tradeoffs: More calls and deeper stacks: the composition pays dispatch and call overhead, which becomes visible on hot paths where the compiler or JIT cannot inline the steps.
The computation is spread over several methods (and often a class), so a reader must jump to follow the flow and can lose the overall picture; debugging steps through more frames.
Decomposition invites over-decomposition: steps that are one-liners shorter than their own signature make the code harder to read than the inline version did.
The benefit depends entirely on the quality of the step names; names like step1, helper or processData make the composition worse than inline code.
Steps must exchange data: through parameters and return values (which grows signatures), or through instance/global state (which hides the sequence's data flow and order dependencies).

participants.responsibility: The short coordinator: its body contains only calls, in order, and its name states the outcome of the whole sequence.
One per operation: performs a single identifiable step at the same level of abstraction as its siblings, and stays private or module-scoped unless it is genuinely reusable.
The object the steps operate on; self-sends keep the sequence and the state it manipulates together without threading a context object through every call.

use_cases: Use-case and orchestration methods: a service method that reserves, charges and confirms, where each call is a named domain operation.
Algorithm phases: a parse/validate/normalise/emit pipeline written as one call per phase, with the phase bodies kept private.
Base-class skeletons: a public method that calls protected hook methods so subclasses refine steps without touching the sequence (the skeleton side of Template Method).
Test setup and fixture building, where each named step can be reused or invoked individually by a test.
Migration and reporting scripts that must be reviewed by someone other than the author: top-down step names let a reviewer approve the sequence without reading every body.
CQRS command and query handlers: a command handler that loads an aggregate, validates, persists, and publishes an event — each phase is a named step, and the macro method is the command's public API.
State machine transitions: a transition method that guards, updates state, and emits a domain event, where each concern is a step method that can be overridden in subclasses.
Build and deployment pipelines: a deploy step that validates, builds, stages, and promotes, written as a sequence of named method calls that mirror the runbook.
Data-processing ETL steps: extract/transform/load written as a macro method, with each step independently testable against a fixture.

Python's standard-library unittest framework: TestCase execution composes fixture setup, test invocation, result collection, and teardown behind named lifecycle methods, while the test runner remains the coordinator.

Spring Framework's AbstractApplicationContext.refresh(): preparation, bean-factory refresh, post-processor setup, singleton initialization, and finish hooks form an ordered lifecycle that subclasses refine.
LLVM's new pass manager: PassBuilder.buildPerModuleDefaultPipeline composes analysis registration, pass-manager assembly, and ordered optimization passes into a named pipeline.
avoid_when: The method really is one expression (a guard, a getter, a single delegation): write the expression and let the name carry the intent.
The steps would need so much shared context that every helper takes four parameters: use a Parameter Object, or move the whole computation into a Method Object.
The code is a chain of pure transformations over one data structure: a pipeline or collection pipeline states the same thing with less ceremony.
A measured hot path where calls are not inlined: keep the details in one method and keep the step names in comments.
anti_patterns: Statement-per-method decomposition: every line becomes its own method, producing a coordinator whose steps are meaningless one-line wrappers.
Step names that describe mechanics instead of intent (step2, helper, processData): the composition then documents nothing and hides the real sequence.
Steps that communicate through hidden instance or global state, so the summary reads as calls but conceals the data flow and the order dependencies.
A macro method that hides control flow or error handling inside its steps, so the visible sequence is not the actual behaviour (steps skipped, errors swallowed).
design_principles: Single responsibility at statement granularity: one identifiable task per method, one level of abstraction for all operations in it.
Intention-revealing naming: names say what a step accomplishes, not how it is implemented.
Encapsulation: step methods stay private or module-scoped and become public only when another caller genuinely needs them.
DRY at the statement level: a named step can be reused elsewhere and changed in one place.
Separation of policy (the sequence) from mechanism (the steps).
best_practices: Write top-down: draft the sequence as calls to steps that do not exist yet, then implement each step - the sequence is the design.
Keep every step at the same level of abstraction, and recurse when a step is itself a composition.
Stop decomposing when a step's body is no longer than its signature, or when the sequence has stopped changing.
Pass data through parameters and return values rather than shared state; when the parameter list grows, introduce a Parameter Object or move the computation into a Method Object.
Keep step visibility as narrow as the language allows, and promote a step deliberately when a subclass or another unit must override it.
Name step methods after the outcome they produce, not the mechanism used: validateOrder instead of checkNullAndLength, fetchFromCache instead of queryRedis.
Watch for a step that exceeds the coordinator in complexity — if its body needs its own macro method, extract it before it grows beyond the coordinator.
Use the IDE's 'method seems to be doing too many things' warnings as a trigger: a macro method approaching 10 steps signals a misplaced abstraction boundary.
Promote a step to a named class or module when it becomes independently reusable or when it needs its own dependencies that the coordinator should not hold.

In test-driven development, write the macro method's signature and step calls first as the test list, then implement each step — this enforces the top-down discipline even without a formal literate approach.
sources: Kent Beck, Smalltalk Best Practice Patterns (Prentice Hall, 1997) - Composed Method (pp. 21-22) and Decomposing Message (pp. 47-48), the top-down method composition this pattern names (the classic image example: Controller>>controlActivity = controlInitialize + controlLoop + controlTerminate).

Martin Fowler, Refactoring: Improving the Design of Existing Code (Addison-Wesley, 1999) — Extract Method (pp. 76-80) is the direct mechanical counterpart; the Composed Method discipline makes extraction redundant in the first pass by keeping methods short enough.

Robert C. Martin, Clean Code: A Handbook of Agile Software Craftsmanship (Prentice Hall, 2008) — Chapter 3 (Functions) codifies the same discipline: functions should do one thing, do it well, and do it only; Martin extends Beck's pattern into a general callable-design philosophy.

Steve McConnell, Code Complete: A Practical Handbook of Software Construction (Microsoft Press, 2004) — Chapter 7 (High-Quality Routines) and Chapter 24 (Refactoring) formalise subroutine decomposition criteria, including when a routine is too short to split.

Ward Cunningham's c2.com wiki — ComposedMethod page records the original pattern description, community discussion, and cross-linkage to related patterns including GoF Template Method. https://wiki.c2.com/?ComposedMethod
